options.a: Routing messages between MS/TP and BACnet/IP networks
options.b: Assigning unique device instances across the network
options.c: Encrypting BACnet traffic between IP subnets
options.d: Broadcast management across IP subnets

distractorExplanations.a: That is a BACnet router's job (network-layer routing between data links); a BBMD forwards broadcasts between IP subnets.
distractorExplanations.b: Device instance numbers are configured per device by the integrator; a BBMD does not assign or manage them.
distractorExplanations.c: Encryption comes from BACnet Secure Connect (TLS), not from a BBMD, which only redistributes broadcast messages.

bms-bas-readiness-check-bacnet-networkin.explanation: Broadcast management across IP subnets. Routers block IP broadcasts, so a BBMD in each subnet forwards BACnet broadcasts such as Who-Is/I-Am to its peers (Broadcast Distribution Table).

options.a: A twisted-pair RS-485 style LAN for BACnet
options.b: An Ethernet-based UDP transport for BACnet
options.c: A free-topology LonTalk channel for LonWorks
options.d: A two-wire 4–20 mA analog loop for sensors

distractorExplanations.b: That describes BACnet/IP (UDP port 47808 on Ethernet), not MS/TP, which runs on an RS-485 twisted-pair bus.
distractorExplanations.c: LonTalk free-topology channels belong to LonWorks; MS/TP is a BACnet data link on RS-485 twisted pair.
distractorExplanations.d: A 4–20 mA loop is a single analog signal circuit, not a multi-drop token-passing LAN like BACnet MS/TP.

bms-bas-readiness-check-bacnet-networkin.explanation: A twisted-pair RS-485 style LAN for BACnet. MS/TP (Master-Slave/Token-Passing) daisy-chains field controllers on shielded twisted pair with end-of-line termination and common baud rates such as 38.4 or 76.8 kbps.

options.a: Alarm floods by suppressing repeat events
options.b: Controller scan time by skipping PID updates
options.c: Wiring runs by sharing one MS/TP trunk
options.d: Polling traffic by eventing changes

distractorExplanations.a: Alarm floods are handled by alarm delays, priorities, and suppression logic; COV only changes how values are reported.
distractorExplanations.b: COV is a network reporting service; it does not change how often a controller executes its PID control loops.
distractorExplanations.c: COV is a software subscription service and has no effect on physical MS/TP trunk layout or cable length.

bms-bas-readiness-check-bacnet-networkin.explanation: Polling traffic by eventing changes. With SubscribeCOV, a device sends a notification only when a value changes by more than its COV increment, instead of being polled on a fixed interval.

options.a: Overshoot from sudden setpoint changes
options.b: Rate of change of the error
options.c: Instant response to current error
options.d: Steady-state error over time

distractorExplanations.a: Damping overshoot on setpoint changes is the derivative term's role; integral action can add overshoot (windup).
distractorExplanations.b: Responding to the rate of change of error is the derivative (D) term, not the integral (I) term.
distractorExplanations.c: Output proportional to the present error is the proportional (P) term, which alone leaves steady-state offset.

bms-bas-readiness-check-hvac-control-011.explanation: Steady-state error over time. Proportional-only control leaves an offset from setpoint; the integral term accumulates error over time and keeps adjusting output until the offset is removed.

options.a: Increase dehumidification at part load
options.b: Raise duct static pressure at low load
options.c: Hold discharge air at a fixed 55°F
options.d: Reduce energy while meeting loads

distractorExplanations.a: Raising SAT reduces coil dehumidification, which is why resets are capped by humidity limits; it does not increase it.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses SAT reset with static pressure reset, which lowers (not raises) duct pressure as VAV demand falls.
distractorExplanations.c: A fixed 55°F discharge is the non-reset baseline that SAT reset is designed to improve on at part load.

bms-bas-readiness-check-hvac-control-012.explanation: Reduce energy while meeting loads. Raising SAT at part load cuts chiller energy and VAV reheat, while the highest-demand zone and humidity limits cap how far the reset can go.

options.a: Raise duct pressure to cut VAV hunting
options.b: Hold supply airflow at design max
options.c: Lower chilled water pump head at low load
options.d: Lower fan energy when demand allows

distractorExplanations.a: Static pressure reset lowers duct pressure; excess pressure tends to cause VAV damper hunting rather than cure it.
distractorExplanations.b: Holding design maximum airflow is the opposite of reset; static pressure reset lets the fan slow as VAV demand drops.
distractorExplanations.c: That is pump differential pressure reset on the water side, a sibling strategy, not duct static pressure reset.

bms-bas-readiness-check-hvac-control-013.explanation: Lower fan energy when demand allows. Trim-and-respond logic lowers the duct static setpoint until the most-open VAV damper is nearly fully open, so the VFD slows and fan power drops roughly with the cube of speed.

options.a: Mechanical cooling running during occupied hours
options.b: Bringing in air that cannot cool economically
options.c: Coil freezing when mixed air drops below 35°F
options.d: Demand-controlled ventilation raising OA on high CO2

distractorExplanations.a: Lockout ends free cooling and hands the load to mechanical cooling; it does not stop compressors from running.
distractorExplanations.c: Coil freeze protection is the low-limit freezestat's job, not the economizer high-limit lockout.
distractorExplanations.d: DCV still raises outdoor air on high CO2 during lockout; lockout only stops economizer free-cooling above the minimum.

bms-bas-readiness-check-hvac-control-014.explanation: Bringing in air that cannot cool economically. High-limit lockout (fixed or differential dry-bulb or enthalpy) returns the outdoor air damper to minimum when outdoor air is warmer or more humid than return air.

options.a: A setpoint deadband that is set too wide
options.b: A derivative term set to zero on the loop
options.c: Normal cycling of a well-tuned PI loop at low load
options.d: Poor tuning, oversized valves, or sensor issues

distractorExplanations.a: A wider deadband reduces cycling; hunting is linked to deadbands that are too narrow or gains that are too high.
distractorExplanations.b: Most HVAC loops run PI with derivative at zero by design; zero D alone does not cause valve hunting.
distractorExplanations.c: A well-tuned loop settles at a steady position; continuous oscillation is a fault symptom, not normal behavior.

bms-bas-readiness-check-hvac-control-015.explanation: Poor tuning, oversized valves, or sensor issues. High gain, an oversized valve working near closed, a noisy or poorly located sensor, or actuator hysteresis all make a loop oscillate.

options.a: They route every alarm to the same on-call pager at equal priority so no fault is ever missed.
options.b: They help operators focus on critical faults and maintain an audit trail of response actions.
options.c: They let alarms clear on return to normal so operators do not need to record any response.
options.d: They satisfy NFPA 72 signaling rules so the BMS can serve as the building's fire alarm system.

distractorExplanations.a: Equal-priority paging creates alarm floods and fatigue; prioritization exists to separate critical faults from nuisance ones.
distractorExplanations.c: Clearing on return to normal without acknowledgment removes the audit trail the acknowledgment workflow is meant to keep.
distractorExplanations.d: NFPA 72 governs listed fire alarm systems; a BMS alarm workflow does not make the BMS a code-compliant fire alarm panel.

options.a: They lower controller CPU load by limiting how often BACnet devices report changes of value.
options.b: They replace trend logs by storing each alarm timestamp as the historical performance record.
options.c: They help operators focus on critical faults and maintain an audit trail of response actions.
options.d: They let operators shelve recurring alarms indefinitely so the alarm summary stays uncluttered.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses alarm workflows with COV increments and subscriptions, which govern how often values are reported.
distractorExplanations.b: Alarm history records discrete events, not continuous values; trend logs are still needed to diagnose performance.
distractorExplanations.d: Indefinite shelving hides real faults; shelving should be time-limited, reviewed, and logged rather than open-ended.

options.a: Equal priority so every alarm pages on-call
options.b: Disabled overnight, including life-safety interlocks
options.c: Engineered so operators see actionable faults
options.d: Configured by the vendor at default factory values

distractorExplanations.a: Equal priority floods on-call staff with nuisance alarms and buries critical faults; priority must be engineered.
distractorExplanations.b: Unoccupied suppression may apply to comfort alarms, but critical equipment and life-safety alarms must stay active.
distractorExplanations.d: Factory defaults do not reflect site criticality or the sequence of operations; priorities must be engineered per site.

bms-bas-readiness-check-platform-ops-011.explanation: Engineered so operators see actionable faults. Priorities, delays, and conditional suppression (e.g., no zone alarms when the AHU is off) prevent alarm floods that hide critical faults.

options.a: Resolution versus storage/network load
options.b: Alarm delay versus operator workload
options.c: Controller scan time versus PID loop gain
options.d: Sensor accuracy versus calibration interval

distractorExplanations.b: Alarm delays are tuned against nuisance trips; trend sample rate is a data-resolution versus storage decision.
distractorExplanations.c: Scan time and loop gain affect control stability; trend sampling is a separate historian setting.
distractorExplanations.d: Accuracy and calibration interval are maintenance trade-offs, not what trend sample rate selection balances.

bms-bas-readiness-check-platform-ops-012.explanation: Resolution versus storage/network load. Fast intervals catch hunting and short cycling but fill storage and add polling traffic; COV or 1–15 minute intervals suit most points.

options.a: A single 24/7 occupied command per AHU
options.b: Occupied/unoccupied and holiday exceptions
options.c: Fixed start times with optimal start disabled
options.d: Overrides that run without an end time

distractorExplanations.a: Running 24/7 wastes energy and drops the unoccupied setback that schedules exist to provide.
distractorExplanations.c: Optimal start is a standard energy measure; fixed early starts waste energy on mild days and start late on extreme ones.
distractorExplanations.d: Overrides without an expiry leave equipment running indefinitely; timed overrides are the accepted practice.

bms-bas-readiness-check-platform-ops-013.explanation: Occupied/unoccupied and holiday exceptions. Weekly occupied/unoccupied periods plus calendar exceptions for holidays and special events stop equipment running on days the building is empty.

options.a: Shared operator logins for quick access
options.b: Time limits and audit trails
options.c: Permanent priority-1 manual commands
options.d: Verbal approval with no written record

distractorExplanations.a: Shared logins break accountability because overrides cannot be traced to a person; each operator needs an account.
distractorExplanations.c: BACnet priority 1 is reserved for Manual Life Safety; operator overrides normally use priority 8 and should expire.
distractorExplanations.d: Verbal approval leaves no audit trail; overrides should be logged with user, reason, and expiry time.

bms-bas-readiness-check-platform-ops-014.explanation: Time limits and audit trails. Timed overrides release on their own, and the audit log records who commanded what, when, and why, so forgotten overrides do not waste energy or mask faults.

options.a: Static equipment images without live values
options.b: Alarm counts without point values
options.c: Vendor logos and floor plans as the main view
options.d: Current values, setpoints, and modes clearly

distractorExplanations.a: Static images show layout but no live state; operators need current values to diagnose equipment.
distractorExplanations.b: Alarm counts alone do not show how far a value is from setpoint or which mode the equipment is in.
distractorExplanations.c: Branding and floor plans add context but are not the operational data that graphics should put first.

bms-bas-readiness-check-platform-ops-015.explanation: Current values, setpoints, and modes clearly. Good graphics put live values beside setpoints, show occupancy and override status, and flag points in alarm or manual so operators can act fast.

options.a: Graphic links and colors before wiring checks
options.b: Sensor/actuator wiring and direction before sequences
options.c: Sequence logic before any field wiring tests
options.d: Network IP and BACnet device instance assignments

distractorExplanations.a: Graphics review is a later front-end task; point-to-point checkout proves field wiring and device response first.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the order: wiring and device direction are proven before functional sequence testing begins.
distractorExplanations.d: Addressing is a network checkout step; point-to-point verifies each sensor and actuator end-to-end.

bms-bas-readiness-check-integration-comm.explanation: Sensor/actuator wiring and direction before sequences. Each input is compared to a reference reading and each output is stroked to confirm direction, range, and fail position before functional testing.

options.a: The unit starts and runs on its local panel
options.b: Each device's vendor ID and model are reported
options.c: Trend files stay within the storage limit
options.d: Control logic matches the written SOO

distractorExplanations.a: Start-up at the local panel is a pre-functional check; SOO testing proves the automatic control logic.
distractorExplanations.b: Vendor ID and model come from device discovery, not from testing the control sequence.
distractorExplanations.c: Trend storage is a historian setting; it does not show that the control logic follows the written sequence.

bms-bas-readiness-check-integration-comm.explanation: Control logic matches the written SOO. Functional tests force each mode (occupied, unoccupied, economizer, failure/safeties) and compare the system's response with the written sequence of operations.

options.a: Estimated kWh from nameplate ratings
options.b: Protocol gateways/mapping with scaled units
options.c: Unscaled raw register values as-is
options.d: Pulse inputs left uncalibrated against the meter

distractorExplanations.a: Nameplate estimates are not metered data; meter integration reads actual registers through a gateway or driver.
distractorExplanations.c: Raw registers often need multipliers, CT ratios, or unit conversion; unscaled values give wrong readings.
distractorExplanations.d: Pulse inputs need the correct pulse weight checked against the meter display, or totals drift from billing data.

bms-bas-readiness-check-integration-comm.explanation: Protocol gateways/mapping with scaled units. Meters on Modbus, M-Bus, or pulse outputs are mapped into BACnet objects with correct multipliers, CT ratios, and units, then verified against the meter display.

options.a: Addressing, binding, power, and actuator status
options.b: AHU discharge air setpoint and economizer mode
options.c: Zone thermostat calibration and heating setpoint
options.d: Duct static pressure reset logic at the AHU

distractorExplanations.b: Upstream AHU settings change supply air conditions but do not explain a box that ignores its own commands.
distractorExplanations.c: A miscalibrated sensor shifts control, but a box that ignores commands points to communication, power, or actuator faults.
distractorExplanations.d: Static pressure reset affects available airflow, not whether a box controller accepts and acts on its commands.

bms-bas-readiness-check-integration-comm.explanation: Addressing, binding, power, and actuator status. A VAV box that ignores commands usually has a duplicate MAC or device instance, a lost binding, no 24 VAC, or a failed or slipping damper actuator.

options.a: Logged, assigned, and closed with evidence
options.b: Closed once the contractor says it is fixed
options.c: Reported verbally at the final walkthrough
options.d: Cleared by a controller reboot and retest

distractorExplanations.b: Closing on a verbal claim skips verification; issues close only after a retest documents the fix.
distractorExplanations.c: Verbal reports at walkthrough leave no tracking record; issues belong in a written Cx issues log.
distractorExplanations.d: A reboot can mask the symptom without fixing the cause; the issue still needs logging and root-cause closure.

bms-bas-readiness-check-integration-comm.explanation: Logged, assigned, and closed with evidence. The commissioning issues log records each deficiency, the responsible party, and the retest or trend evidence used to close it.
